ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Rheumatology Consultation — Flannery O'Connor — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.displayName: Follow-up encounter
code.originalText: Diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus with the rheumatology consultation the same day; vaccinations before immunosuppression

code.displayName: Reason for referral (narrative)

text.paragraph: Inflammatory polyarthritis with fevers, fatigue, a malar-pattern rash, leukopenia, lymphopenia, mild anemia and thrombocytopenia, and protein and blood in the urine in a woman of 25. I suspect systemic lupus erythematosus with kidney involvement rather than rheumatoid arthritis. Please confirm the diagnosis, assess the kidneys, and plan treatment with her. [S]
Urgency: Urgent, within ten days, because of the urine findings. [S]

list.item: Does she have systemic lupus erythematosus, and which tests confirm it and define organ involvement?
Do the urine findings mean lupus nephritis, and does she need a kidney biopsy?
What treatment do you recommend, including hydroxychloroquine, how to keep glucocorticoids low, and which immunosuppressive or biologic drugs?
Which vaccinations and infection screening should come before immunosuppression?
What contraception is suitable, and how should a future pregnancy be planned?
How should bone health, avascular necrosis, and the eyes be protected and monitored?
She knows that her father had lupus: how should that family history shape her counseling?

code.displayName: History of Present illness Narrative

text.paragraph: Ms. O'Connor is seen at the request of Dr. Pemberton-Diallo. For three months she has had symmetrical pain and swelling of the hand joints, wrists, and knees with an hour of morning stiffness, evening fevers, fatigue, a facial rash after sun, some hair shedding, and a painless sore on the roof of her mouth. She has no chest pain on breathing, breathlessness, leg swelling, seizures, or headaches. She had an operation for a floating kidney some years ago. Her father had lupus. She takes only acetaminophen. She asked to hear everything directly and plainly. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Mary Flannery O'Connor was born in Savannah, Georgia, on March 25, 1925, the only child of Edward Francis O'Connor and Regina Cline O'Connor. She later dropped her first name for her writing. [D]

Her father was diagnosed with lupus in 1937; his illness began with a whitish patch of skin on his forehead and arthritis, and was first diagnosed as rheumatoid arthritis. He died of systemic lupus erythematosus in 1941, a month after his 45th birthday, when she was 15. [D]

O'Connor graduated from Georgia State College for Women in 1945 and then studied at the Writers' Workshop of the State University of Iowa, where she earned a Master of Fine Arts; she was writing her first novel by the late 1940s. [D]
In December 1949, at 24, she fell seriously ill on a holiday visit to Georgia and spent about a month in hospital, where she had an operation for a floating kidney. [D]

Evaluation note

list.item: Systemic lupus erythematosus (M32.19). ANA 1:640 meets the EULAR/ACR entry criterion, and the weighted criteria score 32 (fever, thrombocytopenia, acute cutaneous lupus, joint involvement, proteinuria, low C3 and C4, anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm), so she is classified as having lupus; anti-dsDNA 186 and anti-Sm 42 are highly specific. Disease activity is high (SLEDAI-2K 23). The arthritis of lupus mimics rheumatoid arthritis, which is why it is often misnamed. Antiphospholipid antibodies and lupus anticoagulant are negative. [S]

Kidney involvement (R80.9). A protein-to-creatinine ratio of 1.8 g/g with dysmorphic red cells and a red cell cast and normal creatinine almost certainly means lupus nephritis. A kidney biopsy is needed now, because the class decides treatment. [S]

Treatment. Hydroxychloroquine for every patient with lupus, at 5 mg/kg or less, now. If the biopsy shows class III or IV nephritis: three days of pulse methylprednisolone, then prednisone from about 0.5 mg/kg tapered to 5 mg a day or less by six months, with mycophenolate 2 to 3 g a day plus a second agent, either belimumab or a calcineurin inhibitor such as voclosporin, continued for years after a complete response. An angiotensin receptor blocker for proteinuria and blood pressure. If the class were V alone, the plan would change. [S]

Vaccination and infection. Non-live vaccines are best given before immunosuppression: PCV20 and recombinant zoster can be given today and influenza was given in October. She is immune to hepatitis B by vaccination and negative for hepatitis C and HIV. Pneumocystis prophylaxis can be considered while the prednisone dose is high; sulfonamides are best avoided in lupus. [S]

Contraception and pregnancy. Mycophenolate causes birth defects and needs highly effective contraception. With negative antiphospholipid tests, estrogen is not contraindicated by clotting risk, but an intrauterine system is the most effective choice during active disease. Pregnancy should wait for at least six months of quiet disease on compatible medicines. [S]

Bone, avascular necrosis, and eyes. High-dose glucocorticoids threaten bone and can cause avascular necrosis of the hip, especially at high doses. A DXA at the start, vitamin D and calcium, and the lowest glucocorticoid dose protect her; new hip, groin, or knee pain needs prompt MRI. Hydroxychloroquine needs a baseline eye examination with OCT and visual fields within the first year. [S]

Family history. Lupus clusters in families, and first-degree relatives have a much higher relative risk, although the absolute risk to any one relative is low. No genetic test is needed. She was told that treatment and outcomes today are very different from those of earlier generations. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Pemberton-Diallo's referral and the blood and urine tests from nine days ago; the ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, complements, antiphospholipid antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, repeat urine protein-to-creatinine ratio, and urine microscopy drawn here this morning, which returned this afternoon; hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, and pregnancy tests. [S]

code.displayName: Plan of care note

list.item: Hydroxychloroquine 300 mg daily now, long term; baseline eye examination within the first year, then yearly from five years. [S]
Ultrasound-guided kidney biopsy within days. [S]

For class III or IV nephritis: methylprednisolone 500 mg daily for three days, then prednisone 30 mg tapered to 5 mg or less by six months; mycophenolate mofetil, 500 mg twice daily for a week, then 1000 mg twice daily; and belimumab or voclosporin, chosen with her. [S]
Losartan 25 mg daily, with potassium and creatinine in two to four weeks; blood pressure below 130/80. [S]
PCV20 and recombinant zoster dose 1 today, zoster dose 2 in one to two months, seasonal influenza and COVID-19; no live vaccines. [S]
Levonorgestrel intrauterine system before mycophenolate, with a negative pregnancy test. [S]
DXA at the start of glucocorticoids, vitamin D3 and dietary calcium; report hip, groin, or knee pain. [S]
Daily sun protection; no NSAIDs; blood counts weekly for the first month on mycophenolate, then less often; urine protein, sediment, creatinine, and serology every three months. [S]
Every result to be explained to her directly, with a written copy, and shared only with the people she names. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Pemberton-Diallo the same day. Ms. O'Connor was told the diagnosis directly, has a written summary, and agreed to the biopsy and the plan; she will hear the biopsy result from this clinic by telephone first. [S]

Follow-up: Kidney biopsy in two days; this clinic will give her the result and start treatment at the primary care visit in one week, then see her every three months with weekly blood counts in the first month. [S]
